newsitem.title: USA: U.S. record industry launches anti-drug effort.
newsitem.headline: U.S. record industry launches anti-drug effort.

text.p: Countering criticism that the music industry has popularised drug use by condoning it among musicians, the Recording Industry Association of America announced its first united anti-drug effort on Monday.

The RIAA said the move extended the individual efforts of record labels to provide rehabilitation by granting $2 million over three years to the Musicians' Assistance Programme, which runs drug treatment centres and halfway houses.

"I'm proud of the work our companies have already done privately on this issue," RIAA president Hillary Rosen said. "Unfortunately, label reticence to come forward on such a private and confidential matter has to some been misconstrued as industry denial. This is clearly not so," she said.
The RIAA represents the six major record conglomerates, which account for more than 90 percent of all U.S. record sales.

After recent drug-related deaths in rock bands, including those of Jonathan Melvoin of Smashing Pumpkins, Sublime singer Bradley Nowell and Blind Melon singer Shannon Hoon, the industry came under political fire this election year.

Several record label executives were also angered by Michael Greene, president of the National Academy of Recording Arts & Sciences, the 11,000-strong professional organisation that presents the annual Grammy Awards.

NARAS recently launched a separate, much-publicised campaign against drugs in the industry, and Green has accused music companies of denying the problem exists. His efforts, including the establishment of an industry hotline, have drawn backing from about 260 people but not many high-level record executives.

"The labels are obviously upset with Michael Greene and his tactic of trying to embarrass us into responding," one record industry executive, who asked not to be identified, said. "The labels have been involved with this issue since Day One but have been concerned with keeping the issue as confidential as possible," the executive said.

Several other industry sources said they were annoyed by Greene's statements but noted that the effort by the RIAA was not intended to replace Greene's efforts. "This initiative is meant to supplement Michael Greene's MusiCares effort, not supplant it," Tim Sites, a spokesman for RIAA, said.
So far, the six major music groups have provided about $1.5 million for MusiCares.
Hailing the RIAA announcement, Greene said: "We look forward to co-operating with them. This looks like a step in the right direction."
